summary: A Chinese question word stands exactly where the answer will stand — nothing moves to the front and the verb does not change places (‘in situ’): 你喝茶。→ 你喝什么？ ‘What do you drink?’; 安娜是医生。→ 谁是医生？ ‘Who is a doctor?’. Write the answer sentence, then replace the unknown part by the question word. No 吗 is added: the question word already makes the question. The words: 什么 what, 谁 who, 谁的 whose, 哪里 / 哪儿 where, 什么时候 when, 怎么 how (the way), 怎么样 how is it / what is it like, 为什么 why, 几 how many (a small number, with a measure word), 多少 how many / how much (any number), 哪 + measure word which. Time, manner and reason words stand before the verb: 你什么时候吃早饭？ 你为什么不吃肉？

Answer (statement)
Question
rows: 哪里 nǎli / 哪儿 nǎr — where
什么时候 shénme shíhou — when
几 jǐ — how many (small, + measure word)
多少 duōshao — how many / how much
blocks.caption: The question word takes the place of the answer

blocks.title: In situ — the question word stays put
blocks.text: German brings the question word to the front (Was trinkst du?). Chinese leaves it in the object slot: 你喝什么？ (literally ‘you drink what?’). Only when the question word is the subject does it stand first — because the subject stands first anyway: 谁要咖啡？

blocks.title: No 吗 with a question word
blocks.text: 你喝什么？ ‘What do you drink?’ — with 吗 the question word turns into ‘anything’: 你喝什么吗？ ‘Do you drink anything?’. A question has either a question word or 吗, not both.

head: Where it goes
Question words
Example
rows: 谁, 什么, 哪 + MW
谁做饭？ 哪位是警察？
什么, 谁, 多少 / 几 + noun, 哪 + MW
你要哪个？ 她有几个孩子？
那个人是谁？ 这些是谁的？
什么时候, 怎么, 为什么, 在哪里
你什么时候吃早饭？ 你在哪里工作？
blocks.caption: Same slot as the answer

items.title: 几 jǐ
points: a small number is expected (under about ten)
always with a measure word: 几个孩子, 几本书
a child’s age: 你几岁？ the family: 你家有几口人？

items.title: 多少 duōshao
points: the measure word may drop: 多少人, 多少书

items.title: 怎么 + verb — how (the way)
points: 这个怎么吃？ How do you eat this?
怎么 + 不 = how come: 你怎么不喝茶？

items.title: 怎么样 — how is it? how about it?
points: 你妈妈怎么样？ How is your mother?
我们喝茶，怎么样？ Let’s have tea — OK?

blocks.title: Asking about jobs
blocks.text: 他是谁？— 他是我哥哥。他是医生。 The everyday job question is 你做什么工作？ ‘what work do you do?’ (做 ‘to do’) or 你是做什么的？ — answer 我是护士 (no 一位 for yourself).

blocks.title: Polite ‘who?’ and adults’ age
blocks.text: On the phone or to a stranger say 您是哪位？ — 你是谁？ sounds blunt. Ask a child 你几岁？, an adult 你多大？ (an older person 您多大年纪？).

items.def: ‘which’ (3rd tone, with 口) vs ‘that’ (4th tone): 哪本书？ ‘which book?’ — 那本书 ‘that book’.

items.term: 哪里 nǎli ≠ 那里 nàli

items.def: 谁 + 的, built like 我的: 谁的书 ‘whose book’.

askYourself: What do I want to know — a thing, a person, an owner, a place, a time, a way, a reason, a number, a choice?
Write the answer sentence first, then replace the unknown part with the question word.
A number? Small (a child’s age, the family) → 几 + measure word; any size or a price → 多少 (measure word optional).
A choice from a set I can see or name? → 哪 + measure word (+ noun).
The owner? → 谁的 + noun, or 是谁的 at the end.
A time, a way or a reason? → 什么时候 / 怎么 / 为什么 before the verb.
Asking how something is or what it is like? → 怎么样 as the predicate.
Did I add 吗? → remove it.
Did I move the question word to the front? → put it back where the answer goes.
steps: Swap the unknown part for the question word, in the same place.

traps: *什么你喝？ — the object stays after the verb: 你喝什么？
*你喝什么吗？ for ‘what do you drink?’ — with 吗, 什么 means ‘anything’.
*你来什么时候？ → 你什么时候来？ (time before the verb).
*几人, *几书 → 几个人, 几本书 (几 needs a measure word).
你几岁？ to an adult sounds as if they were a child → 你多大？
怎么 asks for the way (怎么去？); 怎么样 asks how something is (这个怎么样？) — not interchangeable.
你是谁？ can sound rude to a stranger → 您是哪位？

quiz.why: The question word stays in the object slot, and there is no 吗.
Time words — also 什么时候 — come before the verb.
几 + 岁 for a child’s age; 岁 is itself the measure word.
哪 needs a measure word; 那 nà means ‘that’.
谁的 stands before the noun, like 我的.
With 吗 the question word becomes ‘anything’.
怎么样 asks how someone or something is; 怎么 needs a verb after it.

quiz.q: Polite on the phone: ‘Who is speaking?’
quiz.why: 哪位 is the polite ‘which person’; no 吗 with a question word.

notes.text: Greek brings the question word to the front (Τι πίνεις;); Chinese leaves it where the answer goes: 你喝什么？
Russian fronts the question word (Что ты пьёшь?); Chinese leaves it in place: 你喝什么？ Russian сколько covers both 几 and 多少; Chinese chooses by the size expected.
Spanish fronts the question word and often inverts (¿Qué bebes tú?); Chinese changes nothing: 你喝什么？
English fronts the question word and adds ‘do’ (What do you drink?); Chinese does neither: 你喝什么？ ‘you drink what?’. *什么你喝？ is the typical mistake.
Colloquial French already leaves the question word in place (Tu bois quoi ? Tu vas où ?) — the Chinese order: 你喝什么？ 你去哪里？
German fronts the question word with the verb in second place (Was trinkst du?); Chinese leaves it in place (你喝什么？).
Hindi leaves the question word in place (तुम क्या पीते हो? ‘you what drink?’), like 你喝什么？ — only the position of the verb differs.
Persian leaves the question word in place (chi mikhori? ‘what are you eating?’, koja miri? ‘where are you going?’), as Chinese does.
Marathi leaves the question word in place (तू काय खातोस? ‘you what eat?’), like Chinese.
Arabic fronts the question word (mādhā tashrabu?); Chinese leaves it in place: 你喝什么？
Hebrew fronts the question word (ma ata shote?); Chinese leaves it in place: 你喝什么？
Turkish leaves the question word in place (Ne içiyorsun? Nereye gidiyorsun?) and adds no question particle to it — as Chinese adds no 吗.
Japanese leaves the question word in place too (何を飲みますか), but keeps か; Chinese drops 吗 when there is a question word.
Korean leaves the question word in place (뭐 마셔요? ‘what do you drink?’), as Chinese does.
Finnish fronts the question word (Mitä sinä juot?); Chinese leaves it in place: 你喝什么？
Hungarian puts the question word right before the verb (Mit iszol?); Chinese puts it where the answer goes, usually after the verb: 你喝什么？
Swahili leaves the question word in place (unakunywa nini? ‘you drink what?’), as Chinese does.
Luganda leaves the question word after the verb (Ogenda wa? ‘you go where?’), as Chinese does: 你去哪里？
Vietnamese works the same way: anh uống gì? ‘you drink what?’ ~ 你喝什么？ — no fronting.
Inuktitut question words (suna ‘what’, kina ‘who’) usually open the sentence, and the verb takes a question ending; Chinese keeps the statement order and changes nothing but the unknown word.

seeAlso.note: German moves the W-word to the front and the verb into second place (Was trinkst du?); Chinese moves nothing: 你喝什么？
Arabic, like German, opens with the question word (mā / mādhā, man, ayna, matā, kayfa, limādhā, kam); kam ‘how many’ takes a singular noun in the accusative, where Chinese 几 / 多少 take a measure word.
Hebrew also puts the question word first (מָה, מִי, אֵיפֹה, מָתַי, אֵיךְ, לָמָּה, כַּמָּה); כַּמָּה covers both ‘how many’ and ‘how much’, like 多少.
